observation.visible_scene: A close-up macro view of a triangular (trilliant-cut) opal cabochon held in a pinch between two fingers above and two fingers below, against a dark, out-of-focus background tinted deep red by the skin. The opal's pale body shows strong play-of-color: bright green, orange, red and yellow patches, plus a small white specular highlight on its domed surface.
visible_changes: The internal color pattern of the opal continuously shifts: large green areas expand and contract, orange/yellow flashes intensify and fade, and occasional blue-violet tones appear (e.g., frames 4, 9, 26, 38), producing a cyclic flashing rather than a one-time change.

The white specular highlight moves position across the stone's dome (top in frame 1, center in frame 2, top in frame 3, lower-left in frame 4, etc.), tracking a small change in the stone's tilt relative to the light.
The stone itself undergoes slight rotational/tilting wobble within the grip: its outline and the orientation of the color bands shift subtly frame to frame, while remaining centered in the frame.
The four holding fingers stay in essentially fixed screen positions throughout, so the apparent motion is the stone tilting in the grip, not the hand traveling across the view.
No camera pan or zoom is evident; the framing and background remain constant, indicating the changes are object motion (tilt) and optical color play rather than camera movement.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the tilt is being driven by the fingers flexing or by an unseen rotation of the stone is not determinable from these frames.
The light source position and the full range of color play outside this 3.2-second window are unknown.
What happens before t=0 and after t=3.2 (e.g., a larger rotation or a stop) is not shown; both ends are mid-motion crop boundaries.
uncertain_details: It is unclear whether the color shifts reflect true physical rotation of the stone or only a change in viewing angle of a static stone under moving light; the two are visually equivalent here.
The exact cut and material identity of the gem cannot be confirmed beyond the visible opalescent play-of-color.
Minor frame-to-frame differences in finger position may be focus/depth-of-field shimmer rather than real finger movement.

do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.

camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from

background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.
